html:
In January 1026 Mahmud of Ghazni sacked the rich temple of Somnath on the coast of Gujarat. It was the most famous of his seventeen or so raids into India.

Mahmud left Ghazni in Afghanistan in October 1025 with about 30,000 horsemen and crossed the Thar desert with water carried on camels. The Chaulukya king of Gujarat fled. The temple's defenders fought for three days and were killed in great numbers. Mahmud broke the Shiva linga, stripped the temple of its gold and went home through Sindh, harassed by local Jats. The loot was put at twenty million dinars.

The raids fed Ghaznavid power and paid for the court at Ghazni, where al-Biruni and the poet Firdausi worked. Persian writers praised Mahmud as a breaker of idols. Sanskrit records of the time say little, and the temple was soon rebuilt; it was destroyed and rebuilt several more times.

Its meaning grew later. In 1842 the British governor-general boasted of bringing back the "gates of Somnath" from Ghazni. In the 20th century the raid became a symbol in Hindu nationalist politics. The present temple was built in 1951 at the urging of Vallabhbhai Patel.
sum: In January 1026 Mahmud of Ghazni sacked the rich temple of Somnath on the coast of Gujarat. It was the most famous of his seventeen or so raids into India.
